title_en: RadioWorld: Transferring World Models to Radio-Frequency Radiance Fields
abstract_en: Electromagnetic (EM) wave propagation in the physical world constitutes a Radio-Frequency (RF) radiance field, providing rich information for 6G communication and sensing. However, existing neural RF field methods suffer from three fundamental limitations: (1) they predominantly rely on per-scene optimization and cannot generalize to unseen scenes; (2) they require costly reference RF measurements in each target scene; and (3) they degrade severely when extrapolating beyond the vicinity of reference measurements. To overcome these limitations, we present RadioWorld, a general framework that adapts a world model to synthesize RF radiance fields directly from physical scene geometry and transceiver locations, without requiring any reference RF measurements at inference. Specifically, RadioWorld couples two specialized modules within a dual-stream Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture: a Scene-Understanding Transformer that encodes 3D scene geometry and transceiver locations to extract environment-aware global EM propagation features, and a Field-Generation Transformer that attends to these features to synthesize the RF radiance field with the local query conditions. We also establish UrbanRF-Bench, a large-scale ray-traced benchmark spanning 657 urban scenes and 32,850 RF radiance fields across seven global cities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RadioWorld significantly outperforms specialized baselines and accurately synthesizes RF fields at arbitrary locations in unseen cities. Code, datasets, and checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.

title_en: ContinuLoc: Continuous Pose Inference over Neural Fields for UAV Geo-Localization
abstract_en: Cross-view UAV geo-localization involves three design choices: how to represent the UAV observation, how to represent the geo-referenced map, and how to infer pose from their interaction. The dominant paradigm organizes the map as a discretized 2DoF candidate library, coupling map representation to pose inference and thus bounding spatial localization precision by candidate sampling resolution. We decouple map representation from pose inference by encoding the geo-referenced map as a continuously queryable semantic neural field, enabling localization to be formulated as explicit optimization over a continuous 4DoF pose space parameterized by 2D ground position, in-plane heading, and viewing scale. Pose hypotheses are evaluated on demand using global descriptors in a shared semantic feature space, bypassing the sampling bottleneck of retrieval. We learn 4DoF pose-sensitive visual representations under full 4DoF supervision provided by ContinuScenes, a multi-city benchmark with dense near-nadir UAV imagery and complete pose annotations. Inference proceeds hierarchically, progressing from broad pose-space coverage to adaptive concentration on high-compatibility regions. Experiments demonstrate substantial gains over representative localization paradigms under progressively stricter 4DoF accuracy criteria. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhouWeikun/ContinuLoc/

title_en: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
abstract_en: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

title_en: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents
abstract_en: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47--90.90\%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46\% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.

title_en: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents
abstract_en: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.

title_en: NANO: Unifying Missingness and Input Uncertainty in Tabular Learning
abstract_en: Missing values are common in tabular data, yet current approaches to handling them often overlook two dimensions. First, an observed value may be uncertain, while a Not-Observed (N.O.) value may still have a reasonable estimate. Inputs should therefore span a continuous spectrum from no evidence to a fully trusted observation. Second, Not-Applicable (N.A.) means that no meaningful value exists for a record, yet this semantic state often lacks explicit representation. To address both dimensions, we introduce NANO, a unified plug-in for input encoding that fits most token-based architectures. Guided by Bayesian evidence weighting, NANO adjusts the influence of a supplied value according to confidence, with all zero-confidence estimates mapped to the same N.O. representation. NANO accepts, but does not require, per-example confidence information during training or inference. For N.A., a separate representation enables models to encode inapplicability and its schema-defined reasons into context. Experiments across eleven datasets and nine backbones show that mixed-confidence training enables a single NANO model to generalize across inference confidence levels, remaining competitive without estimates and improving steadily as estimate reliability and confidence increase. The effectiveness of NANO's handling of N.A. is further demonstrated on three augmented datasets.

title_en: MM-DataLoop: Closing the Data-Side Loop for Recursive Self-Improvement in MLLM Post-Training
abstract_en: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a path toward improving models through repeated evaluation and revision. We study its data side in multimodal language model (MLLM) post-training, where heterogeneous operations and cross-round evidence must be coordinated. MMDataLoop organizes data interventions into five operation families and connects them through an Observe-Diagnose-Plan-Execute-Verify-Reflect cycle with shared rule memory. Across 34 candidate rounds on Qwen3.5-0.8B and five benchmarks, we hold the base initialization, shared training schedule and evaluation protocol fixed while varying data recipes. The five-benchmark mean reaches 63.04 at R33, up 5.32 points from the zero-shot baseline; R29, R32, and R33 form a close top cluster within 0.09 points. In eightcandidate comparisons, guided search reaches the preselected target in six candidates and identifies the top observed candidate, while random arms show higher means and lower dispersion. The selected R29 recipe also scores above two full-pool baselines under the same epoch schedule. Together, these findings establish MM-DataLoop as a traceable workflow and provide an empirical basis for studying how data-side decisions shape outcomes across MLLM post-training recipes.

title_en: Complementary Geometry in Gaussian Splatting
abstract_en: Gaussian Splatting has achieved high visual quality in novel view synthesis, but the accuracy of its rendered geometry remains a challenge. In particular, the rendered depth is computed as an opacity-weighted average along each ray, which may not correspond to the actual scene surface. In this paper, we observe that depth predictions from different views of the same frozen Gaussian representation exhibit complementary errors, allowing us to improve novel-view geometry using information from other views without modifying the original representation. Based on this observation, we propose REVEAL, a general framework that selectively refines novel-view depth using complementary geometric information. Specifically, we first reproject depth predictions from source views to the target view and combine them using robust multi-view consensus. We then introduce a learned selection mechanism to determine whether the candidate depth is more accurate than the original prediction, based on the expected reduction in depth error. In addition, we introduce RIG, a real-world benchmark captured with synchronized RGB-D cameras, which provides ground-truth depth for evaluating both static and dynamic reconstruction models. Experiments on 6 Gaussian Splatting backbones across 3 benchmarks show that REVEAL consistently improves depth accuracy while maintaining comparable rendering quality.

title_en: loopxDINO: Dense Visual Prediction via Iterative Latent Reasoning
abstract_en: Standard dense visual prediction architectures scale representation capacity by stacking deep feedforward decoders (6-16 transformer layers with 50M-200M parameters). This explicit layer stacking brings substantial activation memory overhead during backpropagation, requires high off-chip memory bandwidth for non-tied weights, and uses static computational allocation that cannot adapt to spatial image complexity. We propose loopxDINO, which replaces physical decoder depth with iterative latent reasoning. It has two decoupled components: (1) a frozen DINOv2-Base backbone extracting spatial features in one forward pass and caching static Key-Value representations in GPU memory; (2) a compact weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder (7.96M core, 14.85M total trainable parameters) that recurrently updates queries across T iterations. Recurrence is stabilized by step-conditioned adaLN, LayerNorm-based hyper-ellipsoid manifold regularization, and learnable residual contraction damping. Intermediate mask predictions are fed back as spatial attention biases to guide queries toward ambiguous contours with no extra parameters. On Pascal VOC 2012 semantic segmentation with a single RTX 5060 Ti 16GB GPU, loopxDINO (T=2) achieves 85.66% mIoU and 65.01% Boundary IoU. It outperforms 6-layer DINO-Trans6L (54.06M params) by +1.09% mIoU and +7.41% Boundary IoU with 72.5% fewer parameters. Compared to 4-layer DINO-FCN4L probe (2.43M params, 83.82% mIoU), loopxDINO improves boundary delineation by +6.43% bIoU and occlusion resilience by +6.76% mIoU (60% patch masking). With Adaptive Computation Time (ACT), it reaches 87.3 FPS and retains 29.64% mIoU under 60% occlusion (+5.83% over DINO-Trans6L). Source code, pre-trained weights and evaluation suites are open-sourced under Apache 2.0 at https://github.com/loopxDINO/loopxDINO

title_en: On Adaptive Step Sizes for Eligibility Traces in Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract_en: Many deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms store agent-environment interactions in a replay buffer and later learn by sampling transitions from it. However, this approach can be memory-inefficient and can delay learning because the agent can learn from a transition only when the buffer samples it. Additionally, most of these methods use one-step or short multi-step temporal-difference (TD) updates, which are slow at credit assignment. An alternative approach is to learn from the stream of observations as they arrive without relying on a buffer. Eligibility-trace algorithms allow these incremental updates and can also assign credit over many steps. These algorithms were common with linear function approximation but have only recently been used in deep RL. Basic questions, such as how to use vector step sizes with eligibility traces in the deep RL setting, remain open. In this work, we first show that adaptive vector step sizes must be part of the eligibility trace to keep the equivalence between the forward and backward views. We then show that the step sizes of common optimizers, such as Adam, do not have an online backward view. We introduce a new optimizer, Function-Space Distance (FSD), that maintains the forward-backward equivalence. We test four eligibility-trace algorithms covering semi-gradient and gradient TD updates, as well as value-based and actor-critic methods. We show that FSD performs better than SGD or naively applied Adam. The resulting algorithms outperform or match other streaming methods and are comparable to or better than PPO, which uses a buffer, in most environments. Code available at https://github.com/esraaelelimy/ada_traces

title_en: What Makes Recurrence Generalize Across Lengths?
abstract_en: Multi-step reasoning requires models to preserve and update intermediate information as computation unfolds. State tracking captures this fundamental requirement, but models that succeed within a fixed range of state transitions may not generalize when substantially more updates are required. Recurrent Transformers offer a natural mechanism for addressing this challenge by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, allowing computation to scale with problem length. We study when such recurrent computation generalizes beyond the training range in a controlled state-tracking task, varying operation representation, positional encoding, and recurrent capacity. We find that recurrence alone is insufficient: multi-token template representations and absolute positional encoding can severely limit extrapolation, whereas atomic operation representations enable substantially stronger length generalization. The effect of positional structure also varies with recurrent depth, with periodic positional encoding achieving the strongest mean performance at greater recurrent depth. Most importantly, scaling the recurrent operator extends the extrapolation horizon, reaching 35.1% exact-match accuracy on sequences of 20-40 operations after training only on 2-10, while substantially larger fixed-depth Transformers remain at 0%. Additional recurrent computation at test time can extend the range over which the model generalizes, but does not eliminate failure on much longer sequences. These results suggest that recurrent computation can support length-generalizable state tracking, but that its effectiveness depends critically on whether the learned computation remains reusable across sequence lengths.

title_en: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
abstract_en: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).

title_en: Ziv Meets Sumcheck: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Floating-Point LLM Inference
abstract_en: Zero-knowledge proofs can show that a neural network produced a given output without revealing the network, but current systems for language models prove integer approximations of the model rather than the floating-point arithmetic that is actually deployed. Proving floating-point matrix multiplication has been regarded as hard, because rounding after every addition makes the result depend on the order of the additions. We avoid this obstacle by proving the correctly rounded product, in which every dot product is computed exactly and rounded once. This result is independent of the hardware and at least as accurate as standard kernels. We give an interactive proof for this relation whose cost is close to that of integer matrix multiplication, with roughly a thousand times fewer committed values than per-operation floating-point circuits need constraints, extend it to every layer of a transformer, and give a privacy construction for the complete argument whose zero knowledge we prove under explicit hypotheses. We implement the system and prove the full forward pass of GPT-2 small, including all twelve blocks and the output over the whole vocabulary, in 19 minutes on two processor cores; verification takes 21 seconds. The verifier rejects all 236 attacks we tested, and the model's outputs agree with high-precision inference at least as closely as standard 16-bit inference does.

title_en: DriveTTO: Understanding Search and Selection in Test-Time Trajectory Optimization for End-to-End Driving
abstract_en: In difficult driving scenes, a learned scorer can select a poor trajectory from a fixed pool even when a better candidate is available. Nearby vehicles and road boundaries can also leave only a narrow range of high-scoring maneuvers. These constraints vary with the scene and are difficult to cover exhaustively during training. We introduce DriveTTO, a training-free method that searches around native proposals and checks each proposed refinement against a retained trajectory. A frozen scorer evaluates completed paths at the endpoints they actually reach, guiding resampling in progressively smaller neighborhoods. From a shared reference, one branch draws on planner proposals and another perturbs vehicle controls. DriveTTO blends their poses at matching times and accepts a branch or fusion update only when both frozen scorers predict a gain. On Navtest, DriveTTO recovers nonzero predictive driver model scores (PDMS) in 51.35% of native zero-score cases on average. Accounting for new failures, the zero-score rate falls from 1.63% to 1.13%. Benchmark-specific configurations achieve 95.54 PDMS and 92.30 extended PDMS (EPDMS) on Navtest, 57.10 EPDMS on Navhard, and 40.1 HD-Score on HUGSIM under observed commands. With a single frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on both Navtest and Navhard.

title_en: Unleashing the Value of Raw Point Clouds for 3D Understanding with LLMs
abstract_en: Standard 3D point cloud language models typically rely on pretrained point encoders to extract 3D features and project them into representations processable by large language models (LLMs). However, these encoders are often originally optimized for pre-defined tasks, resulting in a representation bottleneck that may lead to a substantial mismatch with downstream 3D understanding. Moreover, existing models largely follow a single pass closed-book generation, limiting their ability to actively inspect task-relevant 3D regions or retrieve necessary external knowledge. In this work, we present PointTool, an encoder-free and tool-augmented framework for 3D reasoning. PointTool introduces Alignment-Free Patch Tokenization (AFPT) to locally aggregate raw point clouds while preserving fine-grained geometric structure, and Decoupled Point-Text LoRA (DPL) to facilitate global aggregation and 3D knowledge internalization within a frozen LLM. Building upon these designs, Program-Supervised Tool Reasoning (PSTR) enables the model to explicitly operate on raw 3D data and external resources through executable tools, supporting interactive 3D reasoning grounded in spatial evidence. We further introduce PointCloud-TR, a benchmark comprising 13K 3D objects, 39.8K questions, and 35.6K tool trajectories to facilitate training and evaluation of complex 3D reasoning. Experiments demonstrate that PointTool achieves strong performance on both standard and complex 3D understanding tasks, validating the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title_en: PhyCoVE: Benchmarking Physical Counterfactual Video Editing across Diverse Material Dynamics
abstract_en: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how the scene would evolve after the edit. Existing evaluations with counterfactual target videos mainly cover object removal or specific rigid-body motions, although real scenes also involve elastic deformation, fluid flow, and interactions among rigid bodies, elastic solids, and fluids. We introduce PhyCoVE, a benchmark of 533 cases on 110 source videos that covers rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics in five interaction patterns, with edits that remove an object, change a physical quantity, or insert a new object. For the simulated cases, a language model proposes scene designs, coding agents build them with solvers suited to each material and physically based rendering and then simulate each edit from the source scene state, and humans check every stage. For the real cases, we record continuously from one camera position before and after each edit. We also propose counterfactual fidelity, a metric that applies across materials and their interactions and measures how much of the physical change from the source video to the target video a generated video reproduces. We evaluate seven open-source and commercial video editing models and find that counterfactual fidelity ranks them nearly as human preference does, but even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change. The models change how a scene looks but rarely how it evolves, whereas a physical edit requires understanding the dynamics that it changes. Physical counterfactual video editing thus remains far from solved, and PhyCoVE provides a foundation for developing and evaluating methods for it.

title_en: Decoupling Perception from Generation for Agentic 3D CT Report Generation
abstract_en: Chest CT reports repeatedly assess the same anatomical regions for findings and their attributes, such as whether a lung nodule is present and where it is located. These assessments suggest learning to answer visual questions directly, rather than coupling perception to open-ended text generation. Yet current CT report generation models largely follow generic vision-language modeling, which may miss subtle abnormalities when training data are limited. We therefore formulate report generation as a set of visual question-answering decisions coordinated by a large language model (LLM) agent. This decouples visual perception from reasoning and report writing: perception can be learned as a discriminative, non-generative task, while the LLM focuses on reasoning over patient context and posing relevant visual queries. We introduce Rad-VL-JEPA, which unifies report retrieval, finding recognition, and fine-grained attribute characterization through vision-language joint-embedding prediction. Building on this perception module, an agent trained with reinforcement learning (RL) acquires patient-specific visual evidence, while a separate editor incorporates the evidence into the final report, further separating evidence acquisition from report realization. Experiments show that Rad-VL-JEPA achieves strong performance on fine-grained CT understanding tasks with lower amortized per-query inference time than a generative VLM baseline trained with the same CT encoder and VQA data. The resulting reporting system outperforms strong VLM-based and agentic baselines.

title_en: Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation via Topology-Aware Distillation and Progressive Kinematic Reasoning
abstract_en: Hand pose estimation aims to recover the spatial configuration of hand joints from visual observations and serves as a fundamental perception module for downstream systems that rely on complete and topologically consistent hand representations. Most existing methods are developed under the assumption of fully articulated hand structures and tend to produce unstable or implausible predictions when parts of the kinematic structure are persistently absent, resulting in degraded performance or even system failure despite available partial observations. To study this challenge, we construct IncNYU, a physiologically constrained benchmark that simulates structural incompleteness through morphological modification of complete hand models and retains reference locations for both intact and synthetically removed regions. Based on this benchmark, we propose InsHaPE, an Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation framework designed to remain robust under structural incompleteness while preserving performance on standard, fully articulated hands. Built on hierarchical kinematic modeling, InsHaPE introduces two complementary components. First, a topology-aware distillation strategy transfers joint-level and relational priors from fully articulated hand representations, providing anatomically consistent initialization under missing structures. Second, a progressive kinematic reasoning module performs structured inference along the kinematic chain, enabling complete and anatomically consistent pose estimation under severe structural variations. Extensive experiments on NYU/IncNYU, together with external validation on MSRA, demonstrate that InsHaPE improves robustness under structural incompleteness while maintaining competitive performance on complete hands. System-level evaluations further show that InsHaPE improves robustness for downstream applications that require fixed-topology hand pose representations.

title_en: ContextFact: Remembering Facts in Context for Long-Term Conversational Agents
abstract_en: Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. We first study how memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability and evidence access. Reading the entire memory bank reveals gaps that cannot be resolved by retrieval selection alone, showing that some context must be preserved during memory construction. Adjacent-turn grouping improves evidence access at matched unique-turn budgets, while wider windows do not consistently help. This motivates keeping fact-specific context local while organizing cross-session evidence separately. We propose ContextFact, which links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations. Within sessions, it gathers the context needed to interpret each fact. Across sessions, it aligns recurring referents and revisits the source dialogue to reconstruct coherent entity representations linked to the supporting facts. At query time, ContextFact retrieves fact and entity views, reranks them independently, and uses entity-linked expansion to surface related facts; complete entity representations then provide organized cross-session evidence. With Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, ContextFact achieves state-of-the-art performance while using only $21\%$ of the evidence tokens consumed by the strongest evaluated baseline, obtaining $86.49\%$ overall judge accuracy on LoCoMo and $91.00\%$ on LongMemEval-S. Controlled ablations support context-preserving fact boundaries and source-grounded entity reconstruction, while entity readout improves multi-hop accuracy beyond adding more facts.

title_en: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs
abstract_en: Timely access to appropriate medical specialists remains a bottleneck in Bangladesh's healthcare system, as patients describe symptoms in informal Bangla rather than clinical terms, leading to ineffective referrals. This paper compares four model families for predicting medical specialties from Bangla patient narratives: six machine learning (ML) models using hybrid TF-IDF features, four deep learning (DL) models using Word2Vec embeddings trained on the corpus, four fine-tuned transformers, and five large language models (LLMs) evaluated zero-shot. From a corpus of 3798 patient records covering 20 specialties, we retained the five with the most records (Medicine, Gynecology, Dermatology, Pediatrics, Gastroenterology) and split the resulting 2730 records 80:20 into training and test sets shared by all families. The best transformer was XLM-RoBERTa (86.26% accuracy, 86.21% macro-F1), the best ML model was SVM (84.98%, 84.92%), the best DL model was Bidirectional GRU (80.77%, 80.83%), and the best LLM was Gemini (90.29%, 90.15%). Holm-corrected paired McNemar tests show SVM significantly outperforming Bi-LSTM (adjusted p = 0.004), whereas the Gemini-versus-Grok gap does not survive correction (adjusted p = 0.104), and neither the strongest transformer versus the weakest LLM (Grok) nor SVM versus the strongest transformer reaches significance. A tuned classical model is thus statistically indistinguishable from the strongest transformer, so accuracy rankings alone should not be read as evidence of one family's superiority. The findings provide a comparative baseline for Bangla medical text classification.

title_en: VeriLogic: Reinforcement Learning over Verifiable Logical Reasoning Traces
abstract_en: Logical reasoning derives conclusions from premises through explicit intermediate inference steps, providing a natural basis for process-level verification and supervision. However, existing learning methods often rely on response-level outcome signals, which overlook heterogeneous correctness within the reasoning trace: a correct answer may contain invalid reasoning, while valid intermediate steps may also appear in an incorrect response. To address this issue, we introduce Reinforcement Learning on Verifiable Logical Reasoning (VeriLogic), which turns internal reasoning traces into explicit and verifiable learning objects. Rather than treating a response as an indivisible learning unit, VeriLogic decomposes logical reasoning into explicit intermediate judgments, proofs, and final decisions, and organizes them into a unified "Grounding - Optimization - Refinement" pipeline: (1) Verification-Grounded Reasoning Environment Construction grounds logical reasoning into explicit intermediate states and formally checkable proof obligations, making the internal reasoning process accessible to verification and learning; (2) Logical Structured Policy Optimization learns from verifier feedback through complementary global and local rewards, jointly optimizing the overall reasoning outcome while providing targeted optimization signals to different intermediate reasoning paths; and (3) Verifier-Guided Iterative Refinement acts on verifier feedback by leveraging proof states and error messages to iteratively diagnose and repair failed reasoning. Experiments on six logical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over strong baselines, with average improvements of 6.39% and 5.00% on Qwen3 and Llama-3.1. These results highlight the value of making logical reasoning traces verifiable, learnable, and refinable beyond final-answer supervision.

title_en: Group-Balanced Supervised Fine-Tuning for Knowledge-Intensive Domains
abstract_en: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) weights every supervised token equally, so on knowledge-dense corpora the loss budget follows token count rather than importance: on a legal QA benchmark, citation strings absorb 81% of the supervised loss weight budget while the answers being taught absorb 5%. We present Group-Balanced SFT (GB-SFT), which equalizes the loss budget across the semantic roles of tokens within a target sequence. With one tunable dial and one structural switch, GB-SFT contains standard SFT, class- and span-level balancing as corners whose geometry we characterize exactly. On benchmarks in law, medicine, code, and mathematics, we show across model families that: (i) GB- SFT injects new knowledge better than uniform SFT, pointwise token weighting, memory editing, and matched-budget data mixing; (ii) it matches the injection of masking out everything but the knowledge payload while retaining the citation recall that masking destroys (0.98 vs. 0.38); and (iii) role-aware grouping carries the gain: label-free partitions recover at most a third of it, an LLM tagger nearly all where the groups are lexically distinctive; and and (iv) the budget governs what fine-tuning breaks as well as what it learns, acting as a monotone lever on the safety-guardrail erosion SFT causes, at matched task accuracy. We release two new contamination-controlled knowledge-injection benchmarks with validated ground truth.

title_en: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
abstract_en: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

title_en: The Retry Tax: Why Static Same-Task Retries Can Cost More per Completion
abstract_en: Retrying an agent after failure can complete more tasks while increasing the cost per completion. We study a static policy that stops at verified success or an attempt cap and otherwise resets the original prompt and workspace without passing feedback to the next request. Under stationary task success probabilities, independent attempts conditional on the task, and a common attempt cost, easier tasks tend to succeed earlier. When task success probabilities differ, the unresolved mix shifts toward harder tasks. Specializing classical survivor selection, we show that cost per completion is at least as high as in one-shot serving and that marginal cost per additional completion is nondecreasing wherever the completion increments are positive. These are different quantities: one averages spending over all completions, while the other prices the completions added by another attempt. We then arrange each task's existing benchmark runs in different orders, stop each sequence at verified success or the attempt cap, and average the resulting completion and spending at each supported cap. For one OpenHands configuration, replay estimates completion of 59.7 percent with one attempt and 70.0 percent with four, while cost per completion rises from about USD 0.70 to USD 1.32. The recorded trade-off describes fixed configurations on the available tasks. Choosing a cap requires comparing the additional spending with the application's value for the additional completions.

title_en: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery
abstract_en: Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.

title_en: ARC: Adaptive Rollout Control for Efficient Synchronous LLM Reinforcement Learning
abstract_en: Synchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models proceeds through a repeated rollout--barrier--update loop. Each update must wait for a fixed number of complete, group-relative training samples, yet individual response lengths and reward outcomes vary widely and only emerge as generation progresses. Static admission and unconditional completion therefore leave accelerators idle in some steps, and waste computation generating samples that will never contribute to the current update. We present ARC, a closed-loop rollout architecture that governs synchronous RL rollout at group granularity. ARC uses \textit{Calibrated Streaming Backfill} to judge from partial observations whether a group is still worth completing, backfilling a fresh candidate immediately when it is not; \textit{Deferred Group Completion} to park an uncertain early stop and resume it later instead of discarding it outright, bounded by a resume-cycle limit that guarantees termination; and \textit{Adaptive Admission} and \textit{Pipelining} to order admitted samples by early-measured duration and to admit further candidates only while expected supply still falls short of the target number of accepted groups. Under online evaluation, ARC reduces rollout time by $37.4\%$, a $1.60\times$ speedup, and improves effective GRPO throughput by $50.1\%$ over existing baselines, while directly recovering 98.9\% of the training groups that would ultimately have been kept.

title_en: ATLAS: Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival
abstract_en: Dynamic survival prediction requires estimates that reflect a patient's observed clinical history. We introduce ATLAS (Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival), a framework that trains a sequence model on longitudinal data and autoregressively samples possible futures conditional on an individual's covariates and observed history. These trajectories form a patient-specific synthetic cohort from which Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence curves are estimated. We evaluate ATLAS using two stochastic finite-state automaton benchmarks with exact conditional reference curves: a single-covariate process with duration dependence and a late rule change, and a three-covariate Markov process with recovery and competing causes of death. Comparisons include eight direct survival models, including validation-optimized DRSA and Dynamic-DeepHit and history-aware SurvTRACE adaptations, with each neural model trained nine times in the first experiment and five times in the second. After baseline, every ATLAS configuration had lower mean survival-curve error than every fitted direct comparator in both experiments. With a common Sobol sampler and 10,000 trajectories per patient, the best ATLAS model did so in every individual training run, and its mean error was 62% to 84% lower than that of the strongest direct comparator. Baseline advantages were smaller and less consistent in the duration-dependent experiment. ATLAS provides a generative framework for history-conditioned survival estimation, while the accompanying benchmarks enable direct assessment of individual survival and competing-risk predictions against known reference curves.

title_en: Pain Reassessment from Pulse Waveforms with Language Model Explanations
abstract_en: Routine photoplethysmography (PPG) offers a continuous physiological signal for pain reassessment between self-reports. Whether prior recordings provide an individualized physiological reference beyond care-process timing remains unresolved. title_en: RAVEC: Reward-Aligned Visual Evidence Correction
abstract_en: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves multimodal reasoning, but response-level feedback provides limited guidance on which intermediate decisions to correct. Visual interventions reveal sensitivity to image content, yet this sensitivity alone does not establish reward alignment or support across questions. We introduce RAVEC (Reward-Aligned Visual Evidence Correction), which selects visual corrections using local and cross-question reward support and jointly determines their strengths within each response. Paired Visual Evidence Contrast (PVEC) compares predictions from an exponential moving average teacher at the same sampled response prefix under the original image and a version with its annotated evidence region suppressed, yielding signed correction directions. Credit-Risk Allocation (CRA) screens these directions using local reward alignment and reward support from other questions, excluding all responses to the source question. It then solves a response-level budgeted allocation problem, assigning additional cost to directions that locally reduce predictive entropy. The resulting signed visual loss augments Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) during training. Inference uses only the original image and question. Across ten multimodal benchmarks, RAVEC achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared methods with both 3B and 7B Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct models, outperforming GRPO by 2.67 and 1.39 percentage points, respectively. Component ablations support the combined design of evidence alignment, credit qualification, and risk-aware allocation. The project is available at https://yangjj007.github.io/ravec/.

title_en: Supply the Global, Supervise the Local: Combining Representation Conditioning and Alignment in Diffusion Transformers
abstract_en: A pretrained image representation helps train a diffusion transformer in several roles, including as an alignment target, which the model's hidden states learn to match, as in representation alignment (REPA), and as a condition, an extra input describing the image to be generated. Combined, they would give the model an input and a target, but whether they conflict is unknown. To test this, we let the condition carry only part of REPA's target: we split the representation of each image patch into an image-level (global) part, shared by all patches of the image, and a within-image (local) part, the patch's difference from the image-level part, and use one token carrying the image-level part as the condition. Then, the two roles overlap on the image-level part, where they could conflict, while only REPA supervises the within-image part, where we can see whether the token helps REPA. We find that the token and REPA together teach both the image-level part and the within-image part, the main source of REPA's FID improvement, far more than the sum of what each teaches alone, so they cooperate rather than conflict. These findings give one design rule for combining REPA with an image-level condition, supply the global, supervise the local, which we implement as Global-Condition REPA (GC-REPA): REPA with the token as an extra input; the token carries no information beyond REPA's target and is drawn at sampling from a separately trained token prior. GC-REPA greatly accelerates convergence: on ImageNet 256*256, SiT-XL/2 + GC-REPA reaches REPA's 4M- and SiT-XL/2's 7M-iteration FIDs within 200K and 100K iterations (20 and 70 fewer).

title_en: When Can a Rewiring Control Test LLM Weight Readers? C2 and an Eligibility Protocol
abstract_en: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but success could reflect recognition of weight-space regularities (fingerprints) rather than computation, and function-preserving controls cannot tell these apart. We propose C2, a counterfactual that permutes the columns of a network's final linear readout: every other parameter, and the readout's singular values, norms and entry multiset, are unchanged, and the function can change in an exactly recomputable way; we verify that each evaluated permutation does. C2 separates fingerprinting from computation only under three conditions, which we state as an eligibility protocol: a strategy restricted to C2-invariant summaries must already predict the target; C2 must change a property specific to the rewiring; and the reader's identity must be attested. No natural setting we tested is eligible. On tiny MLPs a frontier reader route followed the rewired function on all 24 networks, but invariant baselines were near chance and its backend could not be attested. In two public CNN zoos the conditions traded off: weight statistics predicted CIFAR-10 accuracy in-distribution, but C2's effect on accuracy was not specific to the swap, while per-image targets were specific but not predictable from invariant summaries. On a constructed population where a planted fingerprint rule works, all conditions hold and C2 separates a rule-following reader from an executor. A self-hosted Qwen3.8-27B followed the rewired function rather than the shortcut, and showed no evidence of using the weights with thinking disabled. A registered replication on fresh networks confirmed both findings (tracking minus stuck 0.875, 95% interval [0.750, 1.000]), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B also followed the rewiring (tracking minus stuck 0.729 [0.552, 0.885]). title_en: Decoding Transformer Dynamics via Koopman Subspaces
abstract_en: We apply Koopman operator theory and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to characterise how large language models (LLMs) process different input topics. Treating the layer-to-layer evolution of hidden states as a dynamical system, we fit a linear Koopman operator and take the subspace spanned by its dominant modes as a per-topic spectral fingerprint. Four findings emerge. First, the depth map is near-linear: a single linear operator predicts each next-layer state to within approx. 18% relative error (interior variance explained approx. 0.99). Second, over the 57 MMLU subjects the fingerprint is topic-discriminative, matching the MMLU taxonomy at 0.72 nearest-neighbour purity and each subject's semantic neighbourhood at 0.75 any-hit@3. Third, it is a reproducible signature (split-half self-retrieval approx. 0.97$). Finally, these findings are consistent across seven base models (Qwen2.5 0.5-7B, Llama-3 1-8B), with a suggestive trend of alignment rising with MMLU accuracy. The spectral fingerprint thus provides a probe of how transformers process different topics across depth. Code is available at https://github.com/DeepK/koopman-llm-eacl27.

title_en: Bridging Blind Spots With Words: Decentralized Multi-View Spatial Reasoning via Language-Constrained Communication
abstract_en: As multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) get increasingly used as collaborative partners across embodied robotics, AR/VR, and multi-user systems, spatial reasoning is now often distributed across agents with partial environment visibility, necessitating spatial reasoning integration. Prior work in language-mediated spatial integration is however strictly limited to simplified two-agent scenarios. To address this gap, we first formalize the general problem of decentralized multi-view spatial reasoning, where N agents observe distinct viewpoints, exchange budget-constrained natural language messages, and collaborate to enable a listener to answer spatial queries. We then introduce a novel multi-view spatial benchmark to isolate queries that demand non-trivial multi-view integration. Through an extensive empirical study, we discover that the penalty of restricting decentralized spatial reasoning to natural language with limited budget is far smaller than suggested by prior two-agent literature. Nevertheless, we observe that substantial headroom still remains for multi-agent spatial reasoning in this setting, as evidenced by a significant gap between current centralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling. Moreover, we show that reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially bolsters the decentralized model, effectively closing the gap with the centralized baseline.

title_en: Beyond Evidence Coverage: Encoding-Time Access in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract_en: Cache-sharing multi-agent systems can retain every evidence token's representation while preventing cross-worker access during encoding. With model weights and greedy decoding fixed, we vary distractor layouts using five data-layout seeds per dataset for Qwen3-8B and three for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Supporting access can also outperform full access, but its advantage depends on the model, dataset, and layout. title_en: RES: Accelerating Diffusion Language Models with Rolling Entropy Sampling
abstract_en: A diffusion language sampler makes two choices for every position in its denoising window: where the next token comes from, and when the position is committed to the KV cache. Using the entropy-bound sampler in DiffusionGemma, we study two extremes of the second choice. Committing each token as soon as it is accepted removes the chance to revise it, which hurts when the entropy bound is relaxed to trade accuracy for speed. When accepted tokens are frozen, macro accuracy falls from 73% to 20% as the bound is relaxed, while the unfrozen sampler stays near 70%. Committing a whole block at once wastes computation, since tokens converge in a largely left-to-right order and more than half of the window holds already-final tokens by twenty denoising steps. These findings motivate the Rolling Entropy Sampler (RES), which commits a contiguous accepted prefix once it reaches a minimum length and keeps positions farther ahead open to revision. Unlike earlier rolling samplers, RES runs on uniform diffusion, where accepted tokens can still change, and it needs no training. Across seven benchmarks, RES increases tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, while macro accuracy goes from 80.7% to 78.8%, and it extends the speed-quality Pareto frontier beyond what tuning the entropy bound alone reaches.

title_en: HyperHarness: Learning to Generate Personalized Agent Harnesses from User Histories
abstract_en: Personalized LLM agents rely on an agent harness, the surrounding memory and control code, to connect user history with downstream decisions. Existing methods typically employ either a single shared memory workflow across all users, which is efficient to deploy but cannot adapt how evidence is retrieved and interpreted across diverse histories, or per-user harness optimization, which customizes behavior for each user but requires costly repeated candidate evaluation at deployment and suffers from sparse, noisy supervision in raw logs. To address this trade-off, we present HyperHarness, a framework that learns a shared history-to-harness generator to synthesize executable, user-specific retrieval and answer-guidance code directly from user histories. Given a user's permitted history, HyperHarness prompts a construction LLM to write personalized retrieval and guidance functions, while downstream task scores across training users supervise iterative refinements to the shared generator without reference harnesses or answering-model updates. At deployment, the frozen generator constructs a harness for each unseen user in a single pass from history alone, eliminating per-user task-scored search. Across three benchmarks (PersonaMemv3, Mem-PAL, and MemoryCD) and three answering models (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.8-27B, and GPT-5.6-Luna), HyperHarness achieves the highest aggregate score in seven of nine settings and ranks second in the remaining two, improving over the strongest baselines by up to 5.95 points while cutting matched answer-time tokens by 90.32% over long-context prompting. title_en: Do LLM Agents Compromise Like Humans? Risk and Responsibility in Dyadic Decision-Making
abstract_en: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they must collaborate to make joint decisions. We investigate how this collaboration unfolds under risk, asking whether agents adjust their choices to accommodate their partners, how they assign responsibility for shared outcomes, and whether responsibility attribution shapes subsequent adjustment. We designed a series of agents with systematically varying risk preferences and paired them in a repeated joint decision-making task previously conducted with humans. Like humans, agents converged toward their partners' choices. However, similar aggregate behavior arose from different dynamics: agents showed little evidence of reciprocal adjustment, tended to weigh rewards more, and their responsibility attribution was decoupled from compromise. Similarly, while they showed bias in their responsibility attribution, the outcome's valence shaped the attribution differently than in humans. Our results reveal important differences between human--human and agent--agent joint decision-making, demonstrating that similar social outcomes can emerge from different social dynamics and reasoning.

title_en: Recurrent Point Transformer via Test-Time Training
abstract_en: Real-world point clouds are not naturally bounded: 3D scans grow as sensors move through rooms, LiDAR surveys extend across forest plots, and 4D captures can span thousands of frames. Yet most point-cloud encoders are designed for fixed-size inputs, forcing inference-time cropping or tiling that loses long-range context and requires ad-hoc output stitching. We formulate arbitrary-extent point-cloud segmentation as recurrent sequence-of-chunks processing and introduce PoinTTT, a recurrent point-cloud encoder built on Point Transformer V3 (PTv3). PoinTTT augments PTv3 with residual Large Chunk Test-Time Training (LaCT) layers in both the encoder and decoder. Each LaCT layer maintains compact fast weights as recurrent state: tokens from each chunk update the fast weights, which are then applied to produce chunk features and passed to the next chunk. This design allows PoinTTT to train on fixed-size chunks while processing scenes of arbitrary spatial or temporal extent, with activation memory bounded by the chunk size. A pilot study on ScanNet and nuScenes shows that recurrent TTT improves segmentation over PTv3 baselines. title_en: Grounding Collaborative Agents in Group Cognition
abstract_en: Collaborative agents joining an ongoing team rely on shared context to connect multi-party interaction histories with downstream coordination decisions. Existing work typically focuses either on retrieving historical facts from conversation logs, which surfaces isolated evidence without capturing who knows or owns what, or on evaluating end-to-end interactions, which conflates preparation with execution and lacks direct supervision because a team's history has no single ground-truth summary. To bridge this gap, we formulate group briefing, the task of reconstructing task-relevant group cognition across participants' expressed beliefs, group dynamics, and grounding gaps, and introduce a four-domain benchmark of 1,351 requests and 9,975 verified reference points paired with a two-stage evaluation pipeline combining reference-point coverage and downstream collaboration simulation. Using this pipeline, we show that GroupBrief, a simple task-guided approach that iteratively probes the message history and synthesizes a structured brief without offline memory indexing or graph construction, outperforms ten retrieval and agent-memory baselines in overall coverage with gpt-5.4-mini, while benchmarking nine language models reveals that prospective friction remains harder to recover than past state across model scales. We further use reference-point coverage as a feedback signal for harness optimization, refining GroupBrief's retrieval and synthesis instructions while keeping model weights frozen. On held-out Test projects, GroupBrief (optimized) improves coverage by 2.54 percentage points for gpt-5.4-mini and 12.88 for gpt-5.6-luna, achieving 64.46% and 68.42% preference over no brief in downstream simulations. These results establish our benchmark and evaluation pipeline as a foundation for measuring and optimizing how collaborative agents ground in group cognition.

title_en: LITMUS - Literature Informed Testbed for Mapping Usecases and Synthesizing Risk-Cards
abstract_en: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in real-world applications has heightened the need for systematic, safety-oriented deployment frameworks. Existing approaches typically prioritize the construction of datasets and risk cards around the LLM and AI architecture itself, yet they provide scant consideration for the specific use-case that drives model selection. This omission is problematic because any practical AI deployment begins with a detailed use-case description that informs the assessment of contextual hazards. In this paper, we introduce a structured pipeline that, given a use-case, automatically produces a tailored dataset and an accompanying risk card. The process ensures that identified risks are tightly coupled to the use-case, and it offers traceable evidence from peer-reviewed literature to substantiate each risk to use-case relationship. Prior claim-verification methods (FActScore, FactReasoner) have been validated for factual claims. Risk-relevance is a hypothetical claim about possible harm, and whether evidence retrieval can meaningfully assess such claims remains untested. Literature-Informed Testbed for Mapping Use-cases and Synthesizing (LITMUS) risk cards are the first systematic attempt to characterize this adaptation. We evaluated the pipeline using the MIT Risk Taxonomy and achieved a 0.91 F1-score with a list of 320 samples from the benchmark risk dataset that was considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating robust, evidence-based risk assessments for LLM deployments.

title_en: Do You Even Know What I Want? Improving LLMs Ability to Detect Hidden User Intent
abstract_en: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.

title_en: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM
abstract_en: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.

title_en: T2ISpec: Benchmarking Speculative Decoding for Text-to-Image Generation
abstract_en: Text-to-image (T2I) generators produce detailed images but remain slow at inference. Speculative decoding can reduce this cost, yet its behavior across the rendering requirements of T2I prompts remains insufficiently understood. We introduce T2ISpec, a benchmark of 1,400 prompts balanced across seven rendering topics and two difficulty levels. It evaluates autoregressive and diffusion/flow accelerators by latency, work performed by the target model, and image quality. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) aggregate results hide large differences between topics, (2) alignment and preference scores can disagree with prompt constraint satisfaction, and (3) large reductions in target work can yield limited latency gains. Motivated by these findings, we propose TopicRoute, a plugin that combines prompt routing with speculative and cache controls without retraining the generator. Across six model--method pairs, it achieves a geometric mean speedup of 1.0308x over the native methods, and the speedup carries over to external prompts with the same settings, while quality gains and losses vary across configurations.

title_en: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models
abstract_en: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.

title_en: Mind the Trap As LLMs Guess the Data Model: Grain-Aware Guards Against Fan-out in Text-to-SQL and Its Benchmarks
abstract_en: Text-to-SQL systems built on large language models (LLMs) often aggregate over one-to-many and many-to-many joins, a classic trap: when the joined rows repeat an entity, a SUM or COUNT counts it more than once, yet the query runs and returns a plausible number. We characterize these fan-out errors by one condition on the relation an aggregate reads, which depends on two facts a schema does not show: each measure's grain, and how many rows a join on each key repeats. An audit that tests the condition on the data finds distorted gold answers for 4.2% of the dev questions of BIRD, a widely used benchmark, and BIRD's later, independent revision changed 44% of the answers the audit flags as definite fan-out, against 16% of unflagged ones. We release BIRD-FanOut, 486 BIRD questions with reviewed gold, and GrainTraps, synthetic questions that set this trap and related ones. Across eight LLM agents, functional dependencies (FDs) computed from the data help no more than per-column statistics on GrainTraps, but grain-aware FDs, which also state each measure's grain and the repetition per key, cut fan-out errors on BIRD from 18.4% of runs to about 13%, also on held-out questions and without LLM judges. Accuracy rises less, because most remaining errors are not fan-out and BIRD's hints often prescribe the over-count. Text-to-SQL models should be given the grain of the data, and benchmark gold should be audited on the data. Code, data and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/ahmed-mahran/misqal

title_en: Elicitation format changes zero-shot classification accuracy in a medical vision-language model: a two-center evaluation on colorectal histopathology

title_en: Consumer-Time Validity in Stateful AI Runtimes: Verifying Recovered State and Deferred Authority
abstract_en: Stateful LLM serving engines and agent runtimes reuse execution state and deferred permissions across components and sessions. A cancellation, rollback, or approval is recorded by one component and relied on by another, and recording it does not make the later use valid: a downstream consumer may read state or dispatch an action whose identity, production status, allocation, or target revision has since changed. We call the missing check consumer-time validity and separate two forms. State validity governs what a consumer reads. On vLLM with LMCache, an interrupted KV load leaves unwritten blocks indexed, and a host-only counter rewind desynchronizes the GPU position, so a second tenant generates a schema-valid tool call naming the wrong tenant in 10/10 native-fault runs; the call is recorded and not executed. Authority freshness governs what a consumer executes: on a multi-session approval runtime, an unrevoked deferred grant overwrote a newer revision in one admitted live execution. Output equality cannot test state validity: a fault-free run diverges at token 30 through BF16 batching alone while attended-KV digests match. We therefore specify consumer-bound recovery contracts that, for state recovery, jointly require exclusion, retention, and task completion, and an admissible-witness standard realized as a GPU-free offline trace verifier over scheduler metadata and persisted tool artifacts. On recorded traces the verifier agrees with the reference verdicts in 42/42 frozen GPU-matrix scenarios. An allocation-aware repair satisfies 7/7 triggered vLLM fault predicates on a pinned scheduler-case matrix, where upstream PR 61769 satisfies 2/7, and revision-bound dispatch blocks all 160 deterministic conflicting overwrites in a separate dispatcher cohort. Recovery must be checked where state and authority are consumed, with evidence bound to the consuming request.

title_en: Demystifying Classifier-Free Guidance for Auto-Regressive Image Generation
abstract_en: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) has been widely adopted in autoregressive (AR) models for high-quality image generation. Despite its strong empirical performance, its mechanism in AR models remains unclear. This paper demystifies the mechanism of CFG through both empirical and theoretical studies. By examining the top-ranked semantics of different components in CFG, we show that texture information is primarily encoded in the difference between the conditional and unconditional logits, whereas both logits share previous-token repetition as their leading semantics. This strong repetition semantics obscures the desired texture information, causing greedy decoding from the conditional logits alone to produce nearly pure-color images. Through a training-dynamics analysis of shallow transformers, we prove that this shared repetition semantics does not arise from limitations or failures of pretraining, but instead originates from the texture sparsity of images. We further show that CFG improves generation quality by rectifying this repetition bias during inference. Motivated by the shared semantics between conditional and unconditional logits, we propose Attention Weight Reuse (AttnReuse), which reuses intermediate attention computations from the conditional-logit forward pass to accelerate the unconditional-logit computation. AttnReuse reduces about $25\%$ of attention computation with little performance degradation across different models.

title_en: When Wrong Answers Remain Unsettled: Failure Dynamics in Recurrent Reasoners
abstract_en: When a recurrent reasoner returns a wrong answer, is its computation finished or merely stopped? We test this on a trained Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM; 27M parameters, Sudoku-Extreme) by running the recurrence for one more inference budget and comparing with an unperturbed control. Solved answers persist (0.95 of 512 endpoints). Wrong answers mostly do not: 0.42 of near-miss answers (n=170) and 0.18 of all 512 wrong endpoints keep their answer. Perturbations from 0.05x to 20x the terminal-update scale barely change these rates, so the measurement reflects continued recurrence, not noise sensitivity. The solved-above-wrong ordering also holds in five further settings (a second seed, TRM, Maze, GRAM-guided TRM, N-Queens), but a fixed 1/2 persistence threshold does not, and neither do HRM's endpoint-spectrum and fast-versus-slow predictability patterns, which are not universal diagnostics. Perturb-and-reselect (known from prior work) is consistent with this: frozen noise gains 4.8 accuracy points (197 gained, 2 lost), but compute-matched extended depth gains 5.6 and Sudoku symmetry augmentation 34.6, so noise is not the best use of the budget. Conclusions are limited to finite horizons and one primary HRM checkpoint; they do not exclude asymptotic attractors.

title_en: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever
abstract_en: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.
