title_en: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
abstract_en: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget $k$ (with both end labels fixed when $k$ is odd), the smallest size on which $d$ mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: $d+1$ while $d\le k$, then $2d-k+1$, and beyond $d=\lceil 3k/2\rceil+k-1$ doubling the size adds exactly $k$ mistakes. Unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points correspond to $k=2j$ and size $m+1$, and a single interval gives the thresholds $1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,\dots$. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below $10^5$. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with $O(\log m)$ time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within $0.64$ of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for $m\le70$). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.

title_en: DeCo: Decoupled Traffic State Modeling with Cross-Variable Coordination
abstract_en: Accurate forecasts of traffic flow, occupancy, and speed are essential for congestion management and travel planning. These variables exhibit distinct spatiotemporal patterns, and their coupled dynamics characterize the evolution of traffic conditions, such as the onset and dissipation of congestion. Existing methods often either neglect this coupling or struggle to capture the distinct dynamics of all three variables within a unified model. In this paper, we propose DeCo, a decoupled traffic state modeling framework with cross-variable coordination for forecasting flow, occupancy, and speed. Specifically, DeCo first trains a dedicated forecaster for each variable to specialize in its unique spatiotemporal dynamics. It then estimates a residual correction for each forecast by jointly leveraging the predicted trajectories and recent observations of all three variables, thereby exploiting cross-variable coupling and mitigating systematic prediction errors. We extend the flow-only PeMS03 and PeMS07 benchmarks to all three variables on their original sensors and release the aligned data. Experiments on PeMS03, PeMS04, PeMS07, and PeMS08 show that DeCo achieves the lowest mean absolute error for every variable on every dataset, up to 4.9% below RAGC, the strongest baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/lixus7/DeCo.

title_en: Peel, Don't Whack: Partial Coverage, Imperfect Validators, and Intervention Based Shortcut Mitigation
abstract_en: Without group labels, shortcut mitigation increasingly relies on interventions : label-preserving edits, such as background or watermark replacement, that are proposed automatically and accepted by a validator. Invariance to a complete family of valid edits yields robustness, but in practice coverage is partial and validators err. We analyze both in a stylized linear model. For the population logistic solution and the max-margin limit of gradient descent, the decision on every shortcut-flip group follows one additive rule. Hence worst-group accuracy never decreases with coverage, while individual groups can provably degrade, a mechanism for the Whac-a-Mole effect; full coverage is not always needed. In the logistic regime the validator's false-accept rate must stay below a closed-form tolerance that grows with coverage. With noiseless training data, one false accept can make the max-margin solution ignore the core. In this model, sensitivity-based discovery removes shortcuts in decreasing salience. We also give a model-agnostic certificate, valid under content-independent validation, whose validator-error term comes from an audit. Simulations match the theory, and deep networks on synthetic and real images show the predicted Whac-a-Mole signs, monotone worst-group accuracy and validator fragility. The resulting procedure, Peel (Propose-Edit-Evaluate-Learn), can propose candidate edits from the model's own mistakes. Given an oracle library of the benchmarks' intervention operators, it selects the right ones and beats group-label methods on Waterbirds and UrbanCars. With fully generated edits, run end to end from three discovery seeds, it improves on empirical risk minimization (ERM) on five of six benchmarks but trails exact edits.

title_en: Wavelet-CFM for the extragalactic millimeter-wave sky
abstract_en: We develop a Wavelet-factorized Conditional Flow Matching (Wavelet-CFM) framework to generate fast, accurate simulations of correlated astrophysical fields including gravitational lensing convergence ($κ$), the kinetic and thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ and tSZ) effects, and cosmic infrared background (CIB) emission. Together these make up every bright extragalactic component of the millimeter-wave (mm-wave) sky apart from radio sources. Our approach combines multi-scale wavelet decomposition with conditional flow matching models, trained on $\sim$9$\times$9 deg$^2$ patches at 1-arcminute resolution. The four fields are generated jointly, including their cross couplings, and the model has a tractable likelihood, which to our knowledge has not previously been achieved for this set of components. The power spectra, one-point distributions and Minkowski functionals of the generated maps match a validation set to a few percent. These results show promise for enabling field-level cosmological analyses of mm-wave data.

title_en: Robust Forest-based Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Under High-dimensional Confounding
abstract_en: Understanding how patients with Alzheimer's disease respond differently to treatment is important for individualized therapeutic assessment. Using observational data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we investigate how the association between donepezil dosage and 12-month cognitive performance varies across diagnostic stages and hippocampal volumes. This analysis presents several statistical challenges, including potentially nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity, high-dimensional confounding, and heavy-tailed outcomes with extreme observations. To address these challenges, we develop an Orthogonal Huber Random Forest (OHRF) framework that combines Huber-based robust estimation, Neyman orthogonality, and forest-based adaptive weighting. The proposed method accommodates complex treatment effect heterogeneity while reducing sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors and extreme outcomes. We establish its consistency, asymptotic normality, and finite-sample error bounds. Simulation studies demonstrate favorable estimation accuracy and robustness across a range of error distributions, particularly under heavy-tailed noise and outlier contamination. In the ADNI application, OHRF produces generally narrower pointwise confidence intervals than the conventional Orthogonal Random Forest (ORF) while revealing distinct patterns of treatment effect heterogeneity across diagnostic groups and hippocampal volumes. These findings illustrate the potential of robust, data-adaptive methods for studying heterogeneous treatment responses in complex observational biomedical data.

title_en: Internalized Experience: How Training Data Shapes Memory Formation in LLMs
abstract_en: Parametric memory enables large language models (LLMs) to retain information from past experience and reuse it in subsequent tasks. Yet how training data supports the internalization of reusable task rules remains unclear. We introduce FSMem (Finite-State Machine Memory), a state-transition framework for constructing training data and studying how data content and organization shape memory formation. We evaluate rule reuse across synthetic worlds, classical planning, and code execution through valid-action identification and execution-outcome prediction, complemented by next-operation prediction in code. Our experiments reveal several systematic learning patterns. Under matched training conditions, even unchanged task rules become harder to internalize when learned alongside a larger variety of action types; by contrast, scaling the training data to provide broader state-action coverage generally improves rule learning. We further find that training at a single execution depth produces depth-specialized behavior, with models performing best when training and test executions have similar lengths. Motivated by this finding, we construct cumulative corpora that combine short and long trajectories, which can outperform long-trajectory-only training while using fewer training tokens. Together, these results demonstrate that the same task rules can be internalized differently depending on how execution experience is constructed, and that understanding these learning patterns can guide the design of more effective training data for parametric memory.

title_en: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
abstract_en: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $Ω(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $η=1/H$ requires $Ω(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

title_en: Neural Schrödinger Bridge via Yasue Action with Applications to Generative Modeling
abstract_en: We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schrödinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action functional. This allows us to realize the continuous state evolution by learning the optimal velocity for an ordinary differential equation, as opposed to learning the optimal drift for a stochastic differential equation. The proposed solver only uses the source and the target samples, and not the source and target distributions per se, which makes it particularly suitable for high dimensional applications arising in generative modeling. title_en: Modeling Perceived Promptness in Simultaneous Interpreting from Quality, Structure, and Timing Signals
abstract_en: Simultaneous interpreting requires interpreters to convey the source accurately while keeping pace with it in real time. Timing measures such as segment-onset delay capture part of this requirement, but may not fully reflect how professional evaluators judge promptness. We investigate whether these judgments can be explained by timing alone or whether the interpreted output provides additional information. Our dataset contains 622 Chinese-English and English-Chinese segments from 16 source speeches and seven interpreters. Two senior professional interpreters rated each segment for language quality (LQ), expressiveness (EXP), and perceived latency (LAT), which we also refer to as professional promptness. On held-out source speeches, onset delay alone achieves a Pearson correlation of r = .318 with LAT ratings. Combining predicted LQ and EXP with delay improves the correlation to r = .475. Lexical and structural features provide a stronger signal, reaching r = .632 when combined with delay and r = .658 when predicted quality is also included. These results suggest that professional promptness judgments reflect properties of the interpreted output beyond when the interpreter begins speaking. The additional contribution of predicted quality over structural features, however, is modest. Although the two evaluators differ in how strongly quality relates to LAT, cross-evaluator predictions remain positively correlated with LAT ratings. The overall pattern also holds when each interpreter is held out in turn.

title_en: DRAM: Memory-Efficient Muon via Rank Reallocation in Principal-Random Subspaces
abstract_en: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.

title_en: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
abstract_en: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $μ$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $μ$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $μ$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $μ$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. title_en: Complex band-limited maximum likelihood: estimating the wave behind detected quanta
abstract_en: Detected photons and electrons land at positions drawn from $|ψ|^2$, yet it is $ψ$, phase included, that a wave equation propagates, and the state that produced the particles is often known only in part. A density estimator can recover $|ψ|^2$ directly from the positions, without any wave equation, but it discards the phase, and with it the state. We introduce complex band-limited maximum likelihood (complex BLML), which estimates $ψ$ itself by maximising the likelihood of the detected positions over exactly the intensities the physics allows: squared moduli of complex functions whose spectrum lies in a given set, such as a band, the shape of the aperture, or several modes for a partially coherent source. A single eigenvalue can certify a global maximum. On simulated two-slit far fields we measure what each prior is worth: a band reaches a given accuracy with seven times fewer photons than a kernel density estimate and already gives the fringe contrast and the relative phase, and the shape of the aperture adds the slit geometry. Some quantities need a prior at any number of photons: for slits of one profile the intensity fixes only the contrast $2ρV/(1+ρ^2)$, and on a line two different apertures can produce the same particles. Cutting a pattern to a few fringes, as published records are, removes the slit width. On four public single-particle double-slit records it predicts held-out particles best among the methods we tested, kernel estimators and two-slit optical models included, and it recovers the fringe contrast without a model of the optics. On fluorescent beads it finds the resolution limit of the microscope, $2\mathrm{NA}/λ$, from the photons alone.

title_en: The Curved Exponential Family of Cylindrical Distributions: m-Projection, Curvature and a Test of the von Mises-Fisher Component
abstract_en: Cylindrical data pair a vector in R^d with a direction in S^(m-1). We study a family in which the direction is von Mises-Fisher and, given the direction, the vector is Gaussian with mean affine in it; this generalizes the Mardia-Sutton model. The family is a curved exponential family inside a regular family with Fisher-Bingham directions. We state necessary and sufficient conditions for the maximum-likelihood estimator to exist and be unique. The estimator is explicit except for one scalar root and is the m-projection (Kullback-Leibler projection) of the moment-matching member. Every moment it does not match is a function of one residual, the gap between the sample and fitted second moments of the direction. The squared length of this gap in the Fisher metric is the classical score test of von Mises-Fisher against Fisher-Bingham directions, due to Cox on the circle and extended by Mardia, Holmes and Kent. Specific here are this reading and the exact invariance of its law to the regression part. The exponential curvature lies only in the directions of the regression matrix. In closed form, the information lost on this matrix against the expected information is m-1 observations for uniform directions and (m+1)^2/(m-1) in the limit of high concentration; conditioning on the directions recovers it. Finite mixtures are identifiable. On buoy records the test rejects von Mises-Fisher directions, and generalized von Mises directions raise the held-out log-density by 0.45 nats per observation with one component.

title_en: From atomic events to material degradation across metre and year scales
abstract_en: Material degradation emerges from microscopic events whose consequences accumulate over years, yet mechanism-resolved simulations remain confined below engineering timescales. The challenge is not just the sheer number of events: atomistic evolution is dominated by recurrent local motion, with only a tiny fraction driving lasting structural change. This distinction is not encoded in an instantaneous atomic configuration. Locally indistinguishable states can exhibit different event competition, escape times, and long-horizon outcomes, revealing missing kinetic context as a critical information bottleneck. This context spans space and time: the future consequence of a local transition depends on its surrounding defect environment and the kinetic history leading to its current state. To solve this, AtomWorld reconstructs a predictive kinetic state from multiscale structural observations and trajectory history, distinguishing transient fluctuations from microscopic pathways that drive persistent structural evolution. Learning operates only over transitions admitted by the underlying kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) process, preserving event legality, state evolution, and physical time. Across BCC Fe-Cu precipitation, FCC Ni-Cr-Al ordering, and HCP Zr-H interstitial transport, restoring kinetic context consistently advances persistent evolution while maintaining physical fidelity and transferring to unseen conditions. In irradiated reactor-pressure-vessel steel, this approach achieves up to 420-fold greater persistent evolution under matched event budgets. Combined with scalable execution, it successfully extends mechanism-resolved trajectories to service-year timescales across metre-scale heterogeneous domains.

title_en: Walks2Maps: Learning Indoor Geometry from Crowdsourced Wi-Fi RTT and Motion Trajectories

title_en: State of Mind: Learning and Evaluating World Models of Naturalistic Brain Dynamics
abstract_en: Understanding naturalistic brain activity requires going beyond the stimulus alone, as external inputs continuously interact with an individual's evolving brain state. A world model captures such dynamics in a latent state by inferring it from neural observations, predicting stimulus-driven evolution, and updating with new observations. However, existing brain world models fail to maintain a persistent latent state over time, and standard metrics of neural prediction accuracy cannot tell whether a model tracks an individual's brain state or relies solely on the stimulus. To directly test state inference, prediction, and updating, we introduce BrainStateBench, which evaluates a model's latent state through a frozen linear probe on whole-cortex, movie-driven fMRI. Its State task tests whether a model captures trial-to-trial variability in an individual's responses to repeated stimuli, while Forecast and Updating evaluate future activity predictions without and with new observations, respectively. To track individual brain state across time, we propose Spectator, a linear latent world model trained with a joint-embedding predictive objective. Spectator encodes short- and long-horizon observation histories into a two-timescale latent state and predicts state transitions linearly from the current state and stimulus. Stimulus-only encoders reach 0.320 in fMRI prediction correlation without observing the brain (0% on State), while prior deep brain world models reach 0.239 yet score at most 0.4% on State. In contrast, Spectator achieves 0.349 correlation alongside 5.5% on State, 16.0% on Forecast, and 20.3% on Updating, outperforming all baselines while forecasting over 20x faster than deep forecasting models.

title_en: An equivariant classical density functional for ionic fluids at complex interfaces
abstract_en: Predicting the combined effects of ionic packing and long-range electrostatics at complex interfaces is technologically important, but remains challenging without atomistic simulations. title_en: Asynchronous Uplink Rate Splitting Multiple Access
abstract_en: We study a two-user uplink system in which each user splits its message into layers and transmits them with deliberately chosen timing offsets, a scheme we call asynchronous rate splitting (A-RS). We show that timing offsets make the layers distinguishable only in the excess band of the pulse, where two spectral aliases overlap. For a root-raised-cosine pulse, the rate for every subset of layers has a scalar closed form that depends on the offsets through a single timing dispersion term. For fixed layer spectra and timing offsets, the achievable two-user rate region is a pentagon. Its two maximum-sum-rate corners are attained by successive interference cancellation that combines all matched-filter outputs at each decoding stage. Two layers per user, separated by half a symbol, are optimal for any delay between the users, and the spectrum of the user decoded last is a water-filling nested inside the water-filling of the total power. At high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the optimal spectrum has twice the density in the excess band. By using the excess bandwidth of the pulse, which synchronous transmission leaves unused, A-RS achieves rate pairs outside the regions of both synchronous and asynchronous non-orthogonal multiple access. We implement a practical system with low-density parity-check codes which gives the weaker user $0.97$ bits per symbol more than any single-stream scheme at the same SNR.

title_en: Understanding Membership Inference Attacks on EEG Models

title_en: Beyond Gaussian Calibration: Local Inference in Decentralized SGD
abstract_en: Decentralized SGD minimizes a common objective by local gradient steps and neighbor averaging. title_en: Directional Bias in Quantile SGD and Score-Inversion Inference under Dependence
abstract_en: Quantile stochastic gradient descent (SGD) tracks a quantile by comparing each observation with an adaptive threshold, and closely related updates calibrate online conformal sets and drive quantile temporal-difference learning. At stepsizes near $t^{-1/2}$, as used for online inference, the bias is comparable to the standard error and makes an SGD-based interval miss mostly on one side. title_en: Occupancy Planar Patch: Incremental Probabilistic Bounded-Plane Reconstruction from LiDAR Data
abstract_en: Online surface reconstruction from LiDAR scans requires observation models that respect the sensor's physical measurement geometry. title_en: Two Actions from One State: Fork Futures Teach JEPA World Models to Compare
abstract_en: JEPA world models are trained to predict logged transitions but used to compare counterfactual actions from one state. title_en: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
abstract_en: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). title_en: Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance
abstract_en: We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $α$-moment $ν$ for some unknown $α\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any finite-variance subroutine attaining the sub-Gaussian rate yields the following when the number of samples $n$ is above a suitably defined threshold: Without knowing $α$ or $ν$, we have with probability at least $1-δ$ that $ \|\widehatθ-θ^*\|_Σ \lesssim_α ν^{1/α} \big(\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}\big)^{\frac{α-1}α}, $ where $d$ is the dimension, $Σ$ is the covariate covariance matrix, and $\|v\|_Σ:=(v^\topΣv)^{1/2}$. We further prove a matching minimax lower bound that holds under the same conditions. The reduction is computationally efficient whenever the finite-variance subroutine is. We also obtain a distribution-free prediction guarantee under a bounded raw $α$-moment assumption on the response, and give an analogous $α$-agnostic reduction for mean estimation.

title_en: What Do Differentiable Rule Learners Need? FLARE: Fuzzy Rules with Additive Evidence
abstract_en: Rule learners are used where transparency and accountability are required, because they give practitioners patterns they can read. Learning rules is a discrete problem, so neurosymbolic pipelines that use rules as explanations rely on relaxations such as the straight-through estimator. However, these differentiable rule learners often lag behind both classical rule learners and black-box classifiers in terms of performance. We study which parts of a rule-based classifier affect performance, and how well gradient-based training learns each of them. We found that most of the performance comes from how the rules are weighted: random rules with learned weights are already more accurate than every published differentiable rule learner we tested. Based on our results, we propose FLARE (Fuzzy Learned-Antecedent Rule Evidence), a differentiable rule learner that learns simple rules that combine to make the final decision. We also propose a learned encoding for variables with thousands of categories. We test FLARE on tabular data, using 42 datasets of OpenML-CC18 and the 38 classification tasks of TabArena. On CC18, FLARE exceeds the compared rule learners by 7.69 to 12.38 macro-F1 points and performs comparably to random forests, while remaining 1.00 to 1.11 points below tuned gradient-boosted trees. On TabArena it ranks at the same level as random forests and ahead of the other rule learners. As the concept-to-label head of a concept bottleneck model, FLARE is the best rule-based head in five of six settings. title_en: Variable Importance Recovery in Tabular Foundation Models: A Simulation Study
abstract_en: In machine learning, identifying which variables contribute predictive information can be as important as predictive accuracy. Tabular foundation models have matched or exceeded the predictive performance of tuned gradient boosting trees on many small- and medium-sized tabular datasets. We design and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to compare variable importance recovery across tabular foundation models and established machine learning baselines. Our framework distinguishes multiple population estimands, pairs each one with an aligned model-agnostic importance estimator, and evaluates recovery in terms of ranking, support, and relative magnitude. Our results show that tabular foundation models are generally competitive with established machine-learning baselines in recovering population variable importance, and often more accurate. title_en: eSPG: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Event Speckle Plethysmography
abstract_en: Non-contact measurement of vital signs such as heart rate (HR) is valuable for patient monitoring and rescue operations. However, existing methods struggle with ambient illumination and motion, and have been demonstrated only at distances of tens of meters. Here we introduce event speckle plethysmography (eSPG), which illuminates a body part with a low-power (0.5-5 mW) laser and captures the resulting dynamic speckle pattern using an event camera. Event cameras, with their high dynamic range, temporal resolution, and sensitivity to intensity changes, are well-suited to capturing rapid speckle fluctuations that encode the physiological signal, even under challenging illumination and imaging conditions. We demonstrate HR estimation at 1 km with a mean absolute error of 5 beats per minute, and 90% of estimates satisfy an AAMI-defined HR estimation criterion. This distance exceeds previous remote plethysmography demonstrations by an order of magnitude and previous speckle plethysmography demonstrations by over three orders of magnitude. We also study and characterize robustness to motion and ambient illumination. Our theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that resolving dynamic speckle fluctuations enables accurate heart rate estimation even at kilometer-scale distances, establishing a new direction toward robust, non-contact physiological monitoring.

title_en: SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement
abstract_en: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.

title_en: Speculative Decoding Is Less Speculative Than You Think
abstract_en: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. Building on this observation, we introduce DICE (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples and synchronizes verification randomness across drafting and verification. By combining these known draws with predictions from an existing drafter, DICE allocates computation toward continuations more likely to be used in the current sampling run. This principle guides node selection throughout draft-tree construction and extends to asynchronous prefetching, where DICE predicts which next-round drafts to prepare. Without additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution, DICE achieves state-of-the-art decoding throughput across diverse settings, with speedups of up to 24.6pp over strong baselines.

title_en: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Agnostic PAC Learning for Partial Concept Classes
abstract_en: Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$. This establishes the optimal sample complexity, matching the lower bound of Alon et al. (FOCS 2021).

title_en: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs
abstract_en: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich health information for uncovering latent patient representations and clinically meaningful subgroups. title_en: FairITR: Fairness-Aware Learning of Multicategory Individualized Treatment Rules
abstract_en: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatment decisions based on individual characteristics and can improve treatment outcomes beyond traditional one-size-fits-all strategies. However, similar to other commonly used algorithmic decision-making methods, ITRs without considering model fairness may result in unfair decisions across groups defined by sensitive attributes, such as race or gender. Although extensive methods have been developed for ITR estimation, most focus solely on optimizing treatment outcomes, while research on fairness-aware ITRs remains limited. Moreover, the practical scenario of multicategory treatments is rarely considered in existing fair ITR studies. To address these gaps, we introduce a fairness notion for multicategory ITRs that requires treatment decisions to be independent of sensitive attributes, and then formulate the corresponding problem of estimating fair ITRs. To solve this problem, we further propose FairITR, a fairness-aware learning framework that jointly optimizes treatment outcomes and fairness. FairITR builds on angle-based classification for multicategory ITR learning and integrates adversarial learning with covariance-based regularization to mitigate unfairness in treatment decisions. A theoretical justification for the fairness properties induced by the adversarial debiasing mechanism is also provided. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that FairITR substantially reduces unfairness in ITRs while maintaining competitive treatment values relative to existing baselines.

title_en: Renormalized Entropy from Symmetries: Simplicity Bias and Neural Heat Death
abstract_en: Neural networks have parameter symmetries: parameter transformations that do not affect the represented function. How do these symmetries affect the functions that neural networks ultimately learn? We study the implicit bias arising from these symmetries by calculating the equilibrium distribution over represented functions under Langevin dynamics with Gaussian regularization. To isolate the effect of symmetries on this distribution, we study the limit in which the strength of the regularization is taken to zero. In certain cases, we show that the zero-regularization and infinite-time limits commute. In the low temperature limit, we recover known effective regularizations. At positive temperature, a renormalization procedure allows us to derive a novel entropy which predicts symmetry-induced preference for certain functions. For linear networks, we obtain explicit entropy terms that favor singular and low-rank functions. For networks with homogeneous activations, we find entropy terms that favor inactive neurons, which can lead to neural "heat death" in which equilibrium mass concentrates on networks with vanishing output. We interpret these results through the neural tangent kernel, as a simplicity bias selecting for functions that vary slowly under variations in the parameters.

title_en: $\mathtt{DistP}$: Scaling Local-Update Training with Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
abstract_en: Local-update methods offer a communication-efficient alternative to Distributed Data Parallelism ($\mathtt{DDP}$), but introduce additional hyperparameters that require costly tuning. title_en: Shared Understanding in Human-AI Teams: Coordination Continuity in Evolving Work
abstract_en: People are increasingly working with AI agents as part of extended, asynchronous workflows. In these settings, shared access to information does not guarantee a shared basis for action: goals, plans, and roles may persist while their current significance changes. We introduce coordination continuity, the extent to which collaborators sustain a workable basis for interdependent action as work progresses. Drawing on research on collaborative work, along with two qualitative team studies and a reflexive case from our own repository-based environment, we present a framework of three elements: durable representations of collaborative work; relative coordination properties that support interpretation of representations in the moment; and interaction mechanisms through which the status of representations can be understood and altered. We use a build-act-drift-rebuild heuristic and the notion of consequential moments to characterise when rebuilding may be needed. We draw eight design implications for collaborative AI infrastructure.

title_en: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
abstract_en: Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.

title_en: DPMA: Learning to Compress Mixture-of-Experts Models
abstract_en: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer high computational efficiency, but storing all experts requires substantial memory and limits deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Most retraining-free MoE compression methods commit to either pruning or merging experts, often with a uniform compression ratio across layers. We introduce DPMA (Differentiable Prune Merge Absorb), which jointly learns compression operations and layer-wise expert allocation through gradient descent under a global expert budget. Separate learnable coefficients allow DPMA to prune experts, merge their parameters, and absorb their routing contributions by forwarding routing weights to retained experts. These coefficients and expert assignments are optimised to match the original model's outputs on calibration data while its weights remain frozen. Across four MoE models, eight multiple-choice benchmarks, and five compression ratios, DPMA achieves the highest accuracy averaged over benchmarks and compression ratios on each model among the evaluated methods. At $75\%$ expert reduction, it outperforms the strongest baseline on every model, with gains of up to $6.7$ percentage points.

title_en: Budgeted Subset Selection with a Transferable Learned Value Model
abstract_en: Subset selection is a fundamental task in machine learning, statistics and combinatorial optimisation, with applications in active learning, band selection, input selection and experimental design. The utility of a subset depends on information revealed only after the selection, such as labels or responses, and on interactions among selected candidates. Existing approaches combine value estimation and redundancy control in application-specific ways, which limits their use in other domains. This paper introduces Subset Acquisition with Learned Value Estimates and Search (SALVES), a framework that decomposes subset selection into two components. First, a value model is trained by supervised learning on tasks where the hidden information is known. On a new task, it predicts the utility each candidate would add to the current selection. Second, a selection step chooses the subset from these predictions, typically by simulated annealing with a diversity term penalising redundancy. The value model transfers to new classes, pretrained networks, datasets and sensors, and from synthetic to real data. On the four applications, SALVES matches or outperforms application-specific baselines on average. It requires substantially fewer bands for equal accuracy and remains reliable in input selection where individual baselines fail.

title_en: Energy-preserving Bayesian model reduction: closed-form structured posteriors and probabilistic stability certificates for quadratic operator inference
abstract_en: Bayesian operator inference learns reduced-order models (ROMs) with polynomial structure from state data and returns a closed-form Gaussian posterior over the reduced operators. That posterior is unconstrained, so it gives positive probability to operators with unbounded dynamics, and current practice controls this only through finite-horizon simulation tests on a few samples. We show that energy preservation of the quadratic operator is a set of linear equality constraints, which can be imposed exactly inside the Bayesian formulation without losing the closed form. In particular, the constrained posterior follows from one Kalman-type update of the unconstrained one, and its samples are obtained exactly, by the same correction applied to unconstrained draws. Under this structure, global boundedness for all initial conditions and bounded inputs reduces to a linear matrix condition on the symmetric part of the linear operator. The simulation test is then replaced by a probabilistic stability certificate: the posterior probability that the ROM is globally bounded, estimated with exact confidence bounds; the posterior restricted to certified models is then sampled exactly by rejection. For energy-conserving systems, the linear part can be constrained to be skew-symmetric as well: every draw then grows at most linearly in time, and conserves energy exactly when unforced. On a forced viscous Burgers' equation, the Korteweg-de Vries equation and a two-dimensional viscous Burgers' equation, every sample of the constrained posterior integrates to a bounded trajectory, where up to all unconstrained draws diverge, and beyond the observation window the former is also the more accurate of the two.

title_en: An Asymptotic One-Sample Surrogate for Non-Gaussian ERM with General Convex Regularization
abstract_en: We study convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) with non-Gaussian features and nonsmooth penalties through a surrogate driven by a single Gaussian vector. The surrogate preserves the penalty and calibrates its coefficients using the actual joint law of the feature-label model. We prove that this population calibration exists and is unique. We prove a Gaussian approximation for fresh prediction scores when the data satisfy a Poincaré inequality. Together with regularity conditions on the losses, this approximation yields agreement between the ERM minimizer and its surrogate in normalized means and prediction variances, as well as formulas for prediction and classification risks. The result covers general uniformly strongly convex penalties and pure Lasso under projection anti-concentration. The core proof relies on a cavity Hamilton-Jacobi argument that compares the main statistics of the two minimizers without differentiating the penalty.

title_en: A Spatial Clustering and Resource Allocation Approach for Critical Services in Massive MIMO-Enabled Cellular Networks
abstract_en: In this work, we address the challenge of providing quality-of-service (QoS) guarantees for critical real-time services in cellular networks where both real-time and non-real-time applications must be supported. Leveraging the spatial multiplexing capabilities of Massive Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) technology, we propose a joint clustering and resource allocation framework that limits network interference and enhances the ability to meet the QoS requirements of real-time services while still serving other applications. Our approach begins by clustering active users according to the direction of their channel vectors. Specifically, a downlink probing strategy is employed to group users whose channels lie in the same direction. Channel estimation and the derivation of the corresponding signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) are then performed based on this clustering. Subsequently, we formulate a resource allocation optimization problem across the user groups to satisfy the required QoS for critical real-time services while accommodating the remaining users. We rigorously prove that, in general, finding the global optimum of the resource allocation problem is NP-hard, and for a special case of the formulated problem, we establish a polynomial-time solvable algorithm based on linear programming. We then propose a suboptimal solution for the general problem using a linear relaxation technique. Simulation results are provided to confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approaches.

title_en: A Dual-Mode Protocol for Space-Time-Coding Metasurfaces in OFDM ISAC Systems
abstract_en: Existing integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) frameworks assisted by space-time-coding metasurfaces (STCMs) rely on idealized surface models, which neglect the frequency-selective and angle-dependent response of the meta-atoms, and are typically limited to narrowband single-carrier communications. This paper addresses these limitations by developing a physics-based signal-processing framework for STCM-assisted ISAC systems employing wideband orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) waveforms, which accounts also for beam squint effects across the STCM aperture. On this basis, we propose a dual-mode protocol, in which the STCM operates as a time-varying surface during a short acquisition phase and as a conventional reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) during data transmission. In the acquisition phase, the angle of arrival (AoA) and the composite channel are jointly estimated by maximum likelihood from a single pilot OFDM symbol transmitted over a subset of active subcarriers, together with deliberately introduced virtual carriers; these estimates are then used to configure the RIS for data transmission. Numerical results validate the considered framework and quantify the gains achievable by the proposed dual-mode protocol.

title_en: Passivity Correction of the Thermistor Model in Bolometric Power Sensors and Its Dependence on Bead Temperature
abstract_en: This paper closes a series of works on thermistor bolometric power sensors, coaxial and waveguide, by treating what the two have in common. title_en: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs
abstract_en: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.

title_en: Geometrically Constrained Learning II: Agnostic Proper Learning of Lipschitz Functions
abstract_en: We give a proper learner for Lipschitz functions over the Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given random Gaussian examples labeled by a $λ$-Lipschitz function, $λ\ge 1$, the learner returns a function $h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ that is globally $λ$-Lipschitz and has loss (absolute or squared) at most $\varepsilon$. The sample complexity, running time, and representation size are \[ (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(λ/\varepsilon)}. \] The learning algorithm can be made \emph{agnostic}, given a known bound on the variance of the label marginal distribution. Some known control of label scale is information-theoretically necessary. For arbitrary labels with variance at most $V^2 \ge 1$, the complexity is \[ (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(Vλ/\varepsilon)}, \] and the error is $\mathsf{opt} + \varepsilon$, where $\mathsf{opt}$ is the minimal error among Lipschitz approximators. Our approach combines $L_1$ polynomial regression under a convex gradient constraint with local correction of the Lipschitz property. The learner finds a polynomial that, after smoothing and clipping its range, is very close to a canonical Lipschitz correction of itself, the lower Lipschitz envelope. Our local corrector modifies the lower envelope by replacing distances to sublevel sets with a Gaussian sampling proxy, allowing the construction to be locally and stably estimated from samples.

title_en: Rollout Scheduling for Chaotic Neural ODEs: Coverage Gains, Computational Cost, and Predictive Accuracy
abstract_en: Training Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) on chaotic systems is difficult because small changes in model parameters can lead to rapidly growing differences in predictions. A rollout is a trajectory predicted by the model. Choosing its length from a single global Lyapunov time overlooks differences in local instability. We study rollout scheduling for training on one contiguous rollout per sampled state, asking whether adapting its length to local instability improves prediction. We find the schedule that uses the most trajectory data under an instability budget, a limit on how much instability any one rollout may accumulate. Under stated assumptions, we bound the resulting coverage gain and the coverage lost when the instability estimates are in error. Numerical checks illustrate the theory. Training experiments on Lorenz-63, Lorenz-96, and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky compare adaptive and constant schedules at the same instability budgets and maximum rollout lengths. The budgets are computed from the true system's finite-time Lyapunov exponents. Across the tested settings, adaptive schedules increase trajectory coverage at additional computational cost, without showing a consistent improvement in prediction accuracy. On Lorenz-63, limiting adaptive rollouts to the horizon used to estimate instability improves prediction at the larger budgets. On Kuramoto--Sivashinsky, most configurations provide useful short-time predictions, while all tested long rollouts eventually fail. These findings show why coverage, prediction accuracy, and long-time behavior need separate evaluation, and why instability estimates should be checked over the windows used in training.

title_en: Efficient inference for fairness-constrained sequential decision policies
abstract_en: Adaptive decision systems in education and health choose interventions sequentially and are often required not to leave a protected group too far behind. We study the fairness-constrained optimal value: the largest population value attainable by a policy in a smooth parametric class subject to constraints that are smooth functions of group specific counterfactual functionals, such as value gaps, floors, max-min welfare and budgets. For multi-stage, non-Markov data under sequential ignorability, a sensitivity analysis of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker system shows that this value is pathwise differentiable, with efficient influence function equal to the Lagrangian combination of the influence functions of the group values. The same analysis gives the influence functions of the optimal policy, the multiplier and the group values it delivers. A cross-fitted doubly robust estimator is efficient despite its data-dependent feasible set and yields confidence intervals for the constrained value and the price of fairness. When the constraint binds, any plug-in fair policy violates the population constraint, by a margin that vanishes as the sample grows, with probability tending to one half; tightening the estimated constraint by a one sided confidence margin certifies fairness at a small cost in value. Exact checks, simulations and a synthetic case study illustrate the theory.

title_en: Unlocking Heterogeneous Accelerator Flexibility in AI Data Centers: Sizing and Workload Allocation
abstract_en: AI data centers are an emerging electricity demand, but limited local grid capacity could delay their connection and expansion. While existing operational strategies consider spatio-temporal workload flexibility, few studies address the strategic sizing and allocation of diverse accelerator archetypes with different capital and energy-efficiency trade-offs. The proposed design also eliminates the envelope violations of an unconstrained design at a 0.25\% daily cost increase. These results show how hardware heterogeneity and workload flexibility jointly shape economical, grid-compliant capacity plans.

title_en: Quantum-Informed Regularized Poisson Learning for Graph-Based Semi-Supervised Classification
abstract_en: We introduce IPQSSL, a quantum-informed regularized Poisson framework for graph-based semi-supervised classification under scarce labels. Local graph feature contexts are QR factorized, lifted to unitary encodings, and processed by a shared variational circuit whose measurements yield node wise diagonal weights that stabilize a symmetrized Poisson system. We establish positive definiteness of the symmetrized, regularized operator under explicit spectral conditions and derive a Hermitian, block encoding compatible formulation that separates the classical NISQ oriented implementation from a future fault-tolerant pathway. Across seven benchmarks spanning tabular data and a citation network, the effect of regularization is dataset- and budget-dependent: IPQSSL improves over the Poisson baselines on Iris and Wine at all but the single-label budget, reaching 0.946 accuracy on Iris at ten labels per class and at every budget on German Credit, where, however, all methods remain below the majority class rate. Original Poisson remains preferable on Breast Cancer, Heart Disease, Optdigits, and Cora, with the deficit narrowing as the label budget grows on the two largest graphs. Ablations attribute the gains to diagonal stabilization rather than variational training. The result is a resource transparent bridge between Poisson graph learning and quantum linear algebra, with an explicit empirical delineation of when diagonal regularization helps.

title_en: Adapting AI Weather Foundation Models to a Changing Climate
abstract_en: AI weather foundation models learn from historical archives, while the climate distribution encountered during deployment continues to evolve. This growing model--climate mismatch motivates continual adaptation without repeated full-model retraining, but the structure of weather forecast errors determines how such adaptation should be performed. We develop an online adaptation framework that exploits two complementary error structures: geographically persistent biases and flow-dependent errors that vary with the atmospheric state. Analysis of Aurora-1.3B reveals strongly concentrated forecast-loss sensitivity in its decoder, motivating flow-dependent corrections within fixed low-dimensional sensitivity subspaces. A residual memory tracks persistent errors remaining after this correction, while a variable-wise online gate controls the contribution of the persistent component. We evaluate Aurora-1.3B using ERA5 from 1959--1968 for offline initialization and a strictly chronological 1969--2022 stream for online evaluation, with updates restricted to previously available verification targets. For 2-metre temperature, distributional departure from the historical reference, measured directly from ERA5, is associated with larger frozen-model errors and greater adaptation gains, while the adapted model maintains more stable skill across evaluation periods. Across 69 output fields and five lead times from 6 to 72 hours, our method reduces MSE and MAE by 6.90\% and 6.45\%, respectively, relative to $δ$-Adapter, the strongest of six online adaptation baselines.

title_en: Do DeepONet Trunk-Basis Preconditioners Need Training?
abstract_en: Trunk-basis (TB) preconditioners build the coarse space of a two-level Schwarz preconditioner from the trunk functions of a trained deep operator network (DeepONet), restricted to subdomains. Their effectiveness has been attributed to spectral bias since networks learn low frequencies first, complementing a smoother that removes the high-frequency error. Spectral bias, however, is a property of training, whereas a randomly initialized trunk with a smooth activation is already smooth. We therefore ask whether TB preconditioners need training. In one dimension, we prove that on each subdomain the span of untrained trunk functions is close to the space of low-degree polynomials under suitable nondegeneracy assumptions. Numerically, for the Poisson equation and three-dimensional linear elasticity with constant coefficients, untrained TB and piecewise polynomial coarse spaces of equal dimension yield close conjugate gradient iteration counts, while training with the standard \(\ell^2\) loss sometimes increases them. Training can improve iteration counts when high-contrast coefficients make the low-energy modes non-smooth, and if the loss measures the error in the energy norm. For the Poisson equation with contrast \(10^5\), energy-trained TB coarse spaces need fewer iterations than piecewise polynomials of equal dimension, whereas \(\ell^2\)-trained ones do not. For a topology-optimized elastic cantilever with contrast \(10^6\), the energy-trained TB space enriched with the rigid-body modes gives the fewest iterations at larger coarse dimensions. This suggests that for neural operator-based hybrid solvers, a network's inductive bias and training objective should match the solver.

title_en: Minimax-Optimal Small-Loss Regret in Online Convex Optimization and Applications to Contextual Search and Online Inverse Optimization
abstract_en: We give small-loss regret bounds for online convex optimization (OCO), using one subgradient per round. Let $Δ_T^\star$ denote the cumulative loss of the best fixed decision in hindsight, measured relative to the per-round minima. Our algorithm achieves the regret bound $O(1+\sqrt{Δ_T^\star})$ without knowing $Δ_T^\star$, up to domain and gradient-scale factors. The bound is minimax optimal, including its domain dependence, on $\ell_p$ balls for every $1\le p\le\infty$. No smoothness or condition bounding gradient norms by loss values is assumed, and neither loss values nor the time horizon are needed. Algorithmically, we extend the metric-update revocation of Gupta et al. (2026), originally developed for online inverse optimization, to general OCO using the follow-the-regularized-leader framework and a mixture of multiple base learners. We also apply our algorithm to contextual search and online inverse optimization. In $d$-dimensional contextual search with comparison flips of unknown bias $κ>0$, we obtain minimax expected cumulative absolute error $Θ(\sqrt{d}/κ^2)$ under Euclidean normalization using polynomially many arithmetic operations, resolving an open question of Liu et al. (2021). For online inverse optimization with the Euclidean unit-ball utility domain, our algorithm bounds the regret relative to observed actions by $O(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\sqrt{D_T})$, where $D_T$ is their cumulative suboptimality; this matches the regret rate of Gupta et al. (2026) when $D_T=0$. Our guarantee extends to other utility domains; for example, on the probability simplex, the bound improves to $O(\log(d+1)+\sqrt{D_T\log(d+1)})$.

title_en: Deep Cross-Division Network for Product-and-Ratio Feature Interactions in Industrial Ranking
abstract_en: Learning effective feature interactions is essential for industrial recommender systems. DCN and DCNv2 efficiently automate polynomial feature crossing. However, their cross layers construct interactions using only non-negative integer powers of the input features, with the maximum degree controlled by network depth. Consequently, they cannot directly represent the reciprocal terms required for ratios, rates, and normalized counts unless such features are explicitly provided as inputs. We introduce DCDN, a Deep Cross-Division Network that augments a DCNv2-style cross layer with a division branch. DCDN jointly learns product, ratio, and mixed product-ratio interactions. We characterize the representable interactions as multivariate Laurent polynomials and show that a $K$-layer DCDN generates Laurent monomials of $\ell_1$-order up to $K+1$, with signed degree between $-K$ and $K+1$. We evaluate DCDN against a production-optimized neural-ranking baseline built around DCNv2 and supplied with manually engineered ratio features. Replacing the DCNv2 block with DCDN allowed us to eliminate the entire class of manually engineered ratio features from the model input, reducing the number of input features by $40.1\%$. DCDN is deployed in the production ranking stack of a major short-video service. In a live A/B test on this service, DCDN increased likes by $3.25\%$, shares by $16.26\%$, total view time (TVT) by $0.33\%$, and clicks to open fullscreen by $0.38\%$; all changes were statistically significant. The number of shown videos decreased slightly ($-0.24\%$). These results demonstrate that DCDN can improve user engagement while eliminating reliance on manually engineered ratio features. Our code is publicly released at https://github.com/rw404/DCDN.

title_en: Supervaluationism about vagueness and indeterminacy: A judgment-aggregation perspective
abstract_en: Supervaluationism about vagueness and indeterminacy is based on the idea that some sentences, or predicates within them, have multiple competing interpretations or specifications. A sentence is deemed determinately true if and only if it is true according to all specifications; and determinately false if and only if it is false according to all specifications. In all other cases, the sentence is assigned no determinate truth-value. Supervaluationism, however, is only one way of taking into account the verdicts of different specifications -- in technical terms, "aggregating" those verdicts. In this paper, we introduce insights from the theory of judgment aggregation to study a broad class of different aggregation functions. This allows us to offer an axiomatic characterization of supervaluationism, which, in turn, locates it precisely within a larger logical space of possible approaches to vagueness and indeterminacy. Among other results, we axiomatically compare supervaluationism with subvaluationism, the epistemic theory of vagueness, and Strong Kleene and LP logics.

title_en: Breaking the Barrier of Hard Samples: A Data-Centric Approach to Synthetic Data for Medical Tasks
abstract_en: Data scarcity and quality issues remain significant barriers to developing robust predictive models in medical research. Traditional reliance on real-world data often leads to biased models with poor generalizability across diverse patient populations. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution, yet challenges related to these samples' representativeness and effective utilization persist. This paper introduces Profile2Gen, a novel data-centric framework designed to guide the generation and refinement of synthetic data, focusing on addressing hard-to-learn samples in regression tasks. We conducted approximately 18,000 experiments to validate its effectiveness across six medical datasets, utilizing seven state-of-the-art generative models. Results demonstrate that refined synthetic samples can reduce predictive errors and enhance model reliability. Additionally, we generalize the DataIQ framework to support regression tasks, enabling its application in broader contexts. Statistical analyses confirm that our approach achieves equal or superior performance compared to models trained exclusively on real data.

title_en: Constraint-Aware Anticlustering Decomposition for Certifying Pairwise-Constrained Clustering
abstract_en: Certifying the quality of feasible solutions to large-scale minimum sum-of-squares clustering with pairwise must-link and cannot-link constraints remains challenging, as it requires strong lower bounds on the optimal objective value. We propose a decomposition framework that partitions the data points into smaller subsets, called anticlusters, and solves the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a certified optimality gap for the original problem. To preserve pairwise information, we introduce the Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP), which assigns each connected component of the constraint graph to a single anticluster while seeking geometrically representative subsets. We formulate CAP as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and develop a variable neighborhood search heuristic to construct high-quality decompositions. The resulting lower bound remains valid even when the induced subproblems are not solved to global optimality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets with up to approximately 4,000 observations show that our approach can achieve mean optimality gaps below 1% at a modest computational cost.

title_en: Verifying and Strengthening Neural Tangent Kernel Theory
abstract_en: Writing Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide neural networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime. Its standard proof combines matrix concentration, random Gram matrices, continuous-time dynamics, spectral perturbation, and a bootstrap argument, but has lacked machine-checked verification. We present a Lean\~4 formalisation for two-layer networks, proving an end-to-end theorem: for a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with $σ=\tanh$), frozen biases, paired $\pm 1$ initialisation, and explicit width conditions, gradient flow exists uniquely with probability at least $1-δ$, and $$ \|r(t)\|^2 \leq \|y\|^2 e^{-λ_0 t/2}. $$ The sole data assumption is population NTK non-degeneracy, $λ_0>0$. Initial coercivity, kernel drift, the movement bootstrap, the residual ODE, and flow existence and uniqueness are formally proved. The formalisation also sharpens the standard analysis in two ways. First, replacing the conventional matrix-Bernstein variance proxy with the classical row-covariance proxy yields estimated concentration-width certificates for $\tanh$ that are $36$--$53\times$ smaller at $(m,d)=(16,8)$ and $94$--$121\times$ smaller at $(32,16)$. Lean certifies the inequality; the ratios are numerical. Second, the network Hessian has operator norm $Θ(\sqrt{p})$ on the sup-norm parameter ball (a paper calculation), preventing the expected $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ linearisation bound via sup-norm Taylor estimates. An $L^2$ parameter geometry resolves this issue. Required widths remain polynomial but far beyond practical scales, limiting applicability.

title_en: Practical insights into controlling exponential concentration in quantum machine learning
abstract_en: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models are often limited by exponential concentration, where quantum observables become insensitive to input variations as system size increases. In this work, we provide a comparative empirical study of this phenomenon across Fidelity Quantum Kernels (FQK), Projected Quantum Kernels (PQK), and Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL), within a unified observable-based framework based on expectation-value variance. We investigate how measurement locality, entanglement, and circuit expressivity shape concentration across different architectures. Global fidelity-based kernels exhibit strong concentration driven by Hilbert space dimensionality, whereas local-observable approaches reduce but do not eliminate this effect. In PQK and QEL, concentration is primarily governed by entanglement and quantum dynamical expressivity, with reservoir depth emerging as a key factor in QEL architectures. We further study bandwidth scaling as a general mechanism for controlling encoding expressivity across all models. Our results indicate that bandwidth scaling effectively reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the effective expressivity of the encoding, though this protective effect diminishes in highly expressive structural settings.

title_en: Learned Network Dynamics for Model Predictive Traffic Signal Control under Incidents
abstract_en: Model predictive control (MPC) of urban traffic signals relies on a model of how queues respond to signal decisions, which is hard to specify and calibrate in heterogeneous networks, particularly when incidents change capacities and turning shares. Measurements add a second limitation: the controlled lanes at the stop line are often short, so queues extending upstream of them fall outside lane-level measurements. We propose GNN-MPC, a receding-horizon controller that plans with action-conditioned network dynamics learned by graph neural networks. Phase sequences are coordinated across intersections by approximate best responses, with an acceptance test that keeps the predicted cost no higher than that of the initial plan. In microscopic simulation under non-recurrent incidents, GNN-MPC reduces travel time and increases completed trips relative to all tested controllers, on a homogeneous grid and a heterogeneous 21-intersection network. Controlled comparisons on the heterogeneous network distinguish the roles of observation and prediction. With nearly as many vehicles entering the network, GNN-MPC reduces travel time by 13% relative to MaxPressure with the same upstream measurement, and GNN-MPC without the upstream representation does not reproduce its performance. Under the same traffic measurements, planner and objective, replacing the learned dynamics with calibrated store-and-forward predictors increases travel time by 31-34%. Observing hidden demand and predicting its response to control are thus complementary requirements of network-level predictive control.

title_en: PGS-PCQA: Perceptually Gated Synthetic Supervision for No-Reference Point Cloud Quality Assessment
abstract_en: Existing no-reference point cloud quality assessment (NR-PCQA) methods perform well within individual datasets but generalize poorly across datasets. We identify insufficient distortion coverage in training data as a key cause: on unseen distortion types, models rank severity levels near chance or even in reverse. We propose perceptually gated synthetic supervision for no-reference point cloud quality assessment (PGS-PCQA), an NR-PCQA model trained with synthetic distortion ranking. It builds a synthetic distortion bank from source reference point clouds and uses within-type severity ranking as supervision in addition to the source mean opinion scores (MOS), requiring no subjective scores for the synthetic samples. Since higher severity does not always mean lower perceived quality, a perceptual gate softens the ranking targets of pairs with small perceptual differences in rendered views. The synthetic supervision is used only during training and needs no target-domain data. In a single training run on SJTU-PCQA, PGS-PCQA achieves Spearman rank correlation coefficients (SRCCs) of 0.709 on WPC and 0.751 on BASICS. The corresponding published DSP-PCQA scores are 0.595 and 0.723. Under reference-disjoint cross-validation, PGS-PCQA achieves SRCCs of 0.955 on SJTU-PCQA, 0.934 on WPC, 0.906 on BASICS, and 0.791 on LS-PCQA Part I. In the exclusion experiment, the reported scores for the reduced synthetic bank represent 58-65% of the full-bank SRCC gain relative to training without the bank. Code is available at https://github.com/Fan-QY/PGS-PCQA.

title_en: Beyond Outlier Rejection: Transient-Aware Reconstruction of Multi-Stack MRI
abstract_en: Clinical MRI typically acquires the organ of interest as consecutive stacks of 2D slices in different orientations. Reconstruction methods such as SVRTK and NeSVoR fuse them into one volume and down-weight what does not fit, although in living tissue the change during the scan is often the signal itself and can contain clinically relevant physiological information, such as fetal motion and uterine contraction. We propose an analysis-by-synthesis decomposition that explains every acquired voxel through its exact acquisition geometry as a static anatomy shared by all stacks, a rigid and smooth non-rigid motion per stack, and a sparse transient field per stack for changes during one acquisition only. A robust reweighting keeps such changes out of the anatomy. The model is fitted per subject without training data, with one configuration for all datasets. On a digital phantom with known ground truth, static changes are kept entirely in the anatomy, and the transient field of the stack that saw a transient recovers 68% of it at 12mm radius. From identical inputs, the anatomy predicts held-out stacks better than SVRTK and NeSVoR on uterine (NCC 0.897 against 0.874 and 0.863, 123 patients) and on prostate MRI from unseen sites and scanners (0.847 against 0.795 and 0.757, 85 patients), and on fetal brain MRI as well as SVRTK and better than NeSVoR (0.771 against 0.763 and 0.747, 83 fetuses). The transient fields flag corrupted fetal slices with an AUROC of 0.94 against expert raters. As the input of a frozen anomaly detector trained on healthy subjects only, the anatomy localizes radiologist-delineated uterine lesions better than the SVRTK and NeSVoR volumes (AUROC 0.76 against 0.71 and 0.71, 37 patients).
